profiles.meeting_scenario: At Meridian Harbor Asset Management, a Quant Research Lead and a Product Strategy Manager are holding a planning meeting about how to move a recent research result on discretized Merton portfolio strategies into the firm's next-stage evaluation pipeline for model portfolios. The context is that research suggests the continuous-time myopic strategy performs nearly as well as the discrete-time optimum when rebalancing intervals are sufficiently small, and leadership wants to know whether the idea is worth advancing as a candidate allocation approach for the digital advisory platform. The agenda is to align on the workplan for the next six weeks: which analyses will be run first, what internal reference setup the work should use, how to position the candidate strategy relative to an existing balanced-income sleeve, who owns each workstream, and what milestone should be hit before the August product committee calendar is finalized. The expected outcome is a concrete plan with responsibilities, dependencies, and timing for completing the next-stage package.

members.name: Dana Cho
members.expertise: Portfolio theory, stochastic control, backtesting design
members.background: Dana has a PhD in financial engineering, previously worked on systematic allocation models at a hedge fund, and now leads applied research for Meridian Harbor's model portfolios.
members.private_state: Dana wants to preserve methodological rigor, avoid overselling an academic result before it is properly replicated in-house, and keep the initial work lightweight enough for his small research team to finish this month.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to a 'small test group' for an early-stage strategy, they usually mean an internal audience such as the CIO, two senior portfolio managers, and the model governance working group.

Completing the 'standard validation phase' means finishing the quant team's normal replication-and-robustness cycle: comparing the discretized Merton rule to the discrete-time optimum across step sizes and scenarios.

The 'standard assumptions pack' for early-stage work means the research team's default setup: gross returns, no trading frictions, and total-return index inputs unless someone explicitly asks for implementation overlays.
Saying the strategy fits the 'balanced-income' investor profile mainly refers to a moderate risk-aversion setting similar to the utility parameterization used in his replication notebook.
If a milestone is described as being 'before committee scheduling,' the real objective is to decide whether the idea merits further internal review, not to prepare it for an external-facing test.

members.name: Ravi Patel
members.expertise: Investment product rollout, committee process, advisor platform packaging
members.background: Ravi came from a large wealth platform where he launched managed-account offerings, and now translates research ideas into products that can pass committee, compliance, and advisor enablement.
members.private_state: Ravi wants to secure an August product committee slot, reuse as much existing platform process as possible, and make sure the idea is close enough to launch format that leadership can approve a limited advisor-channel test quickly.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to a 'small test group' for a candidate model-portfolio idea, they usually mean a handful of trusted external advisors using real but limited client allocations under a controlled rollout.
Completing the 'standard validation phase' means getting through the usual decision-readiness gate: enough evidence, framing, and operational clarity for product, compliance, and committee review.
The 'standard assumptions pack' means the product team's committee-ready template with platform fees, slippage, and the house return assumptions already layered in.
Matching the 'balanced-income' investor profile means inheriting the platform's existing retirement-account guardrails such as long-only ETFs, allocation bands, and no leverage.
If a milestone is described as being 'before committee scheduling,' the point is to have something mature enough that he can justify holding the committee slot and tee up a controlled market test.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss getting the strategy in front of a 'small test group' after the next-stage package is done.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the small test group is internal: the CIO, model governance reviewers, and a couple of portfolio managers who will react to the research evidence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the small test group is external: a short list of friendly advisors who can use the strategy in a limited live-channel pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither person hears 'small test group' as something needing definition because both internal review audiences and limited external advisor cohorts are commonly described that way in asset-management organizations; the phrase sounds operationally routine and not like a scope decision.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to finish the 'standard validation phase' before locking the next milestone.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the validation phase is complete when the discretized Merton policy has been shown, in Meridian's own tests, to remain close to the discrete-time optimum across daily and weekly step sizes and several simulated market regimes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the validation phase is complete when there is enough net-of-fee evidence, plain-English rationale, and operating clarity for product and compliance to treat the idea as decision-ready for committee.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'standard validation phase' sounds like established process language, and each function has its own mature internal checklist behind that label; because they are discussing sequencing rather than debating the checklist itself, the mismatch stays submerged.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to run the work under the 'standard assumptions pack.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the research team's baseline procedure: gross-return series, frictionless rebalancing, annualized parameter estimates from total-return data, and no implementation costs unless added later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the product committee template: house capital-market assumptions plus platform fee overlay, 10 bps slippage, and the standard presentation format used for live model portfolios.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each function has its own well-established 'standard' package and neither expects a supposedly standard internal artifact to require clarification, so the phrase passes unnoticed as common ground.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'the balanced-income investor profile' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the strategy should fit the 'same investor profile as the balanced-income sleeve.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this refers to a moderate-risk utility setting from his research work, essentially a representative investor with medium risk aversion in a simple two-ETF allocation problem.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this refers to the existing platform sleeve's operational context: retirement accounts, long-only ETF menu, equity-allocation bands, and no borrowing or shorting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The balanced-income sleeve is an internal shorthand everyone recognizes, but Dana interprets it through the lens of investor preference calibration while Ravi interprets it through platform constraints and account rules.
